sentences: Since 2011 June 11, 2016 By Jovilisi Waqa Rugby Pacific Nations Cup: Fiji Come From Behind To Beat Tonga Share Share this article × X Facebook LinkedIn WhatsApp Reddit Email Copy In the Pacific Nations Cup (PNC) opening match against a tough Tongan side, Fiji have come from behind to win 23-18 to take a dramatic win.

This was the first match of the PNC 2016 round of the World Rugby triangular tournament between Fiji, Tonga and Samoa to determine which side qualifies for 2019 Rugby World Cup , so it is an important series for all three sides.
Pacific Nations Cup: Fiji Come From Behind To Beat Tonga - Last Word On Sports Skip to content LWOS INC About Contact Apply Openings Writing FAQ Ad Policy Last Word On Sports Sports News Since 2011.

Tonga, which has a population of 109,000, had nine debutante players in the team that included Nafi Tuitavake who started at center (a former New Zealand Sevens representative) while Fiji had three new players including the 2014/2015 World Rugby ‘Sevens Player Of The Year’ Samisoni Viriviri running at fullback.

Fiji wins Pacific Nations Cup opener It was tit-for-tat from the start, with the opening points coming from impressive halfback Sonetane Takalua in the 18th minute through a penalty and then spectacularly Pila ‘Iongi beat Adriu Delai one-on-one to cross over in the corner in the 26th minute.

It was the first of the European sides three games on their South Seas Tour –a terrific show of support for the Pacific rugby nations–while the Tier One unions in Europe blatantly refuse to undertake yearly.

The win is a stepping stone to automatic qualification to the Rugby World Cup to be hosted by Japan in 2019, as the top two teams from this year and next year’s 2017 PNC qualifies automatically while the third runner-up must go through a repechage tournament with an European team.

Embed from Getty Images The game was a special one too for the man in control, as it was his 71st international game for Welshman Nigel Owens (pictured) who has now taken over from South African Jonathan Kaplan to be the most capped referee in World Rugby.

While the Tongans still have work-on factors to their game, they will be happy with their first outing of the 2016 PNC and they will build on this as they tackle the touring Georgian International side next week at the same Suva venue, as the build-up match to the Fiji v Manu Samoa PNC game.
#PNC2016 pic.twitter.com/gK18lpuNyS — Fiji Sun (@sun_fiji) June 11, 2016 Fiji XV – 15.

The Toutai Kefu coached Tongan side did everything right in the opening half of this game, taking it to the hosts to lead 0-15 before a pep talk at the breather from the Kiwi ‘mastermind’ of the Fiji team John McKee helped the Flying Fijians recover the result.
The pulsating game brought the 8,000 plus crowd at Fiji’s ANZ Stadium to their feet many times, as Fijian handling errors and some indecision saved the Tongans from what could have been an onslaught.
Fiji came to life in that second 40 minutes, as they got their spark back and were rewarded with a solo effort from Volavola, who cleverly danced his way through defenders to score under the posts.
Such good territory gained, from the lineout Fiji capitalized on loose ball and launched another attack and the Biarritz number eight Nemia Soqeta crashed over.

Fiji was on fire now, with the backline having more clean ball and plenty of line breaks were being made from outside center Vereniki Goneva only to be let down by his supporting players who were nowhere near when the offload was on.
Debutant Eremasi Radrodro gave Fiji the lead for the first time in the game after some good continuity with replacement Suva halfback Seru Vularika.
Great defence gives Fiji the advantage leading into the final PNC round-robin match.
Tonga should be commended for their valiant effort, and head coach Kefu will be happy with his debutantes, especially winger Iongi who ply his trade in the American Rugby Championship .

With Talesa Vaeinu missing from the team, he was a able replacement along with Tuitavake, and those two will be the future of Tongan rugby especially in the backline, where they need depth as they have abundance of forwards coming through every year.
That will be an enormous match and Last Word On Sports will follow all the matches in this triangular tournament.

sentences: Photo credit: Facebook/Fiji Rugby / Ian Williams/ Riley Sports Opinion: The first leg of the 2026 Nations Championship and World Rugby Nations Cup competitions was completed over the weekend.
Fiji joined New Zealand in the Nations Championship, the first such Tier 1 competition the Flying Fijians have been included in apart from the Rugby World Cup.

This came after both Fiji and Japan were granted Tier 1 status by World Rugby last year, elevating them to the top tier of world rugby status and joining world champs South Africa, Australia, Argentina and the Six Nations teams England, France, Italy, Scotland and Wales.

Fiji's flanker Lekima Tagitagivalu (C) and teammates huddle after conceding a sixth try during the Rugby Union Nations Championship match between Fiji and England at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool on 11 July 2026.
AFP / Oli Scarff Flying Fijians The Fiji Rugby Union (FRU) moved the Flying Fijians' three home matches against Wales, England and Scotland to Europe for the July series.
Marcelo Hernandez / World Rugby/World Rugby via Getty Images On the field Samoa and Tonga started their Nations Cup campaigns well and got wins at the start.
And more importantly, what key lessons can they carry forward into the rest of 2026 and towards the 2027 Rugby World Cup?

One thing to remember here too is the FRU had to find its own finances to pay the bills, although World Rugby made allocations for part of the costs via it tour grant to all participating teams in the competition.
Their Drua players would have been the only group playing together regularly for a long period, in this case in the Super Rugby Pacific competition.

The All Blacks got together a week before they took on France too, but the difference for them was the fact that just two of the players in the current squad were playing in Japan, while the others were in the Super Rugby Pacific competition here in New Zealand.
The FRU is not France, Japan or World Rugby.
Contract offers are more lucrative to those who have played for their national teams than for those solely coming out of clubs.

That performance and the overall improvement seen put the team in good stead as they prepare for their upcoming tour of South Africa, where they will also play four Test matches against the world champions.
Moving forward, the Flying Fijians will compete at the Pacific Cup in September against Japan, Canada and the USA and then round off the year with the second leg of the Nations Championship.
The lessons need to be taken on board now, with at least 15 months left to the Rugby World Cup.
Samoa and Tonga competed in the Nations Cup, which also featured Tier 2 teams from Asia, Africa, the Americas and Europe.
So, how did our Pacific sides fare on the global stage?

FRU Board chairman John Sanday said in earlier conversations that money generated from the gatetakings would be used to help the union with its rugby stadium plan, assist in development programmes, and other needs.

At the same time, the FRU used the tour to promote Fiji as a sports tourism destination, with hopes that the home unions would consider joining Scotland, which has been the only team from up North to make tours to Fiji.

Pasifika issue Time together is something Fiji, Samoa and Tonga will continue to battle over the coming years, unless and until all their players are able to play together regularly in a competition somewhere.
Fiji had more than 20 players based in Europe, playing in different competitions, for different teams.
Samoa and Tonga basically had the same setup, with their players in the now defunct Moana Pasifika being the only ones that played together regularly.
Going for them as well was the fact that all their players are professionals who have been tested through and through, and they brought that into the national team setup.
But Fiji was not able to do that, while Samoa and Tonga showed promise early but fizzled out in the end.
Gone are the days when Fiji, Samoa and Tonga had players who were playing solely for family and country.

Players back then wore their national team jerseys with pride, they knew what the vanua (people and country) demanded, what they had to do, and they would leave everything on the pitch for the jersey.
Neither is Lakapi Samoa or the Tonga Rugby Union.
They must also realise they need to be playing for their national teams for their own good.
So, perhaps, the ultimate goal for players should be to play for their national team, as it opens the door to many more opportunities.
For Fiji, Samoa and Tonga going forward, that is a discussion that needs to happen now.
However, they fell short in their next two matches.
Reviews of their matches showed they were in it throughout.
Samoa and Tonga will wait until November for the second round of the Nations Cup competition.
